subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
I would like to submit that the amendment is entirely in order. In doing so I wish first of all to distinguish clearly between the purposes and the principles of the bill. The Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) himself noted the distinction between purpose and principle when in speaking on this measure in the house on March 26 he said as reported on page 1809 of Hansard:
In moving his resolution the minister is not supposed to do more than to state the general purposes of the measure. On the introduction of his bill, when asked, as I understand the rules he should, he may give a succinct statement indicating the general purposes of the legislation, and the principles to be crystallized into legislative form.
I draw attention to the distinction which the Prime Minister very properly made, and at that time drew to the attention of the house,

between the purposes of the legislation and the principles to be crystallized into legislative form. The Prime Minister further said as reported on page 1810:
The motion for second reading will involve the approval or the disapproval of the general principle indicated by the bill.
A little further on he said:
But general legislation, upon which the government has determined its policy, is usually submitted to a committee of the whole house.
And the government pursuing the intention therein expressed has in mind I understand submitting the bill to a committee of the whole house rather than sending it to a standing committee. In other words, the government has decided its policy as it is expressed in the legislation, and there is not open for further discussion in committee the question of policy with respect to its provisions as was the case for example in connection with the bill respecting the creation of a central bank. In that case the Minister of Finance made it quite clear that the question whether there was to bo public or private ownership of shares, or public or private control, was a perfectly open matter, something that could be discussed in the committee to which the bill would be sent. But in this case, in the light of what the Prime Minister has said, the government has indicated by its action in not permitting the bill to go to a standing committee, and the reasons given by the Prime Minister therefor, that the principles embodied in the legislation indicate the government's final policy.
At the time of submitting the amendment I was careful to look up Your Honour's previous rulings in the house, to see that the amendment that was moved would be in order. I would like to read the amendment itself and then Your Honour's latest ruling on a question of order in the case of an amendment on second reading, to see if the amendment does not give ample evidence of being entirely in order. The amendment is:
This house, while prepared to support legislation for assisting the orderly marketing of natural products, is unalterably opposed to the enactment of any compulsory measure which delegates to unnamed and undetermined individuals, groups or organizations, sweeping powers over the production and trade and commerce of the nation, and which confers upon a minister of the crown and upon the governor in council unprecedented authority and unusual powers to restrict production, and interprovincial, inter-imperial, and foreign trade as regards both exports and imports, as well as other autocratic powers.
Your Honour in ruling the other evening in regard to a measure before the house, the last I think on which Your Honour gave a

Marketing Act-Mr. M-ackenzie King
ruling, namely that relating to the freight rates bill, drew attention under standing order 75 in regard to second reading to citation 755, as set forth in Beauchesne which is as follows:
It is also competent to a member who desires to place on record any special reasons for not agreeing to the second reading of a bill, to move as an amendment to the question, a resolution declaratory of some principle adverse to, or differing from, the principles, policy, or provisions of the. bill, ...
My purpose in moving that amendment was to give special reasons for not agreeing to the second reading of the bill, and in so doing I therefore moved an amendment which would be declaratory of some principle which is adverse to the principles and policy and provisions of the bill.
As to what are the principles, policies and provisions of the bill, there can be no mistake, once one looks at the measure. As I have said, the purpose of the bill as set forth in the title is to improve the methods and practices involved in the marketing of natural products and export trade by means of regulation. Regulation is a method, a process, a matter of procedure, not a principle. Regulation is a purpose which all parties in this house hold in common. That is not the principle of the bill, any more than the establishment of a dominion marketing board as such is the principle of the bill. The purpose of the bill is that of regulating and improving production-

The second
reading could be revived later on. The amendment declares, in the meantime, for its being based on a principle that is adverse to that which hon. gentlemen opposite have embodied in the legislation. The amendment would mean that the bill would not now be read a second time et cetera. May I go on and refer to the question of the principle? Without any question the principle of this bill-one of its principles-is to take away from parliament and to entrust to bodies delegated for the purpose the right of making regulations which would have the force of law and be enforceable by fine and imprisonment; to take that power away from parliament itself and give it to other bodies still to be created. That is a principle that from our point of view completely undermines the authority of parliament. It is, I contend, a principle that should be maintained above all others by the House of Commons. But the bill goes still further and gives to the governor in
council power to restrict trade, to prohibit both imports and exports by order in council. Our contention is that the regulation of trade is a duty which should be performed by this parliament, not delegated to any governor in council. The governor in council should have no more right to place an embargo on exports and imports or to restrict importation or exportation of commodities than to do away entirely with the tariff. The control of the tariff should remain with this parliament. The amendment is declaratory in the clearest terms of the assertion of the willingness of the opposition to have parliament pass the necessary measures for the regulation of trade and marketing, but it contemplates having this done by the House of Commons itself, combined, of course, with the Senate.
In case there should be any question whatever as to principles underlying the present bill being those of taking away from parliament control over trade and over production, also over expenditures arising out of the legislation, and being the principles underlying limited production and restricted trade and the creation of monopolies, let me refer specifically to certain provisions; because as the rule I have just read points out, an amendment may declare principles adverse to or differing from the principles, policies or provisions of the bill. These are some of its provisions. Section 3 provides:
(1) The governor in council may establish a board to be known as the dominion marketing board to regulate the marketing of natural products as hereinafter provided.
With this should be read subsection (a) and
(f)	of section 4 which shows how it is "hereinafter provided."
(a)	to regulate the time and place of marketing the regulated product, and to determine the manner of distribution and the quantity and quality or grade of the regulated product that shall be marketed by any person at any time, and to prohibit the marketing of any of the regulated product of any grade or quality;
(f) to require any or all persons engaged in the production or marketing of the regulated product to register their names, addresses, and occupations with the board, or to obtain a licence from the board, and such licence shall be subject to cancellation by the board for violation of any provision of this act or regulation made thereunder;
Then section 5 provides:
(1) A representative number of persons engaged in the production and marketing or the production or marketing of a natural product may petition the governor in council to approve a scheme for the regulation of the marketing of such natural product by a local board under the supervision of the board.
(3) Upon receipt of a report from the board recommending the approval of the scheme as submitted or as amended by the board, the minister may recommend the approval thereof,

and the governor in council may thereupon approve the said scheme and fix the date when the same shall be effective.
Section 6 provides that:
(1)	When a scheme has been approved by the governor in council, the minister shall give public notice thereof in the Canada Gazette.
(2)	The provisions of the scheme as approved shall have the force of law, and the local board shall, from the date of the publication of the said notice of approval, be a body politic and corporate.
And again section 9:
(1)	Notwithstanding that no petition in relation to any natural product has been filed, the minister may, if he is satisfied that the trade and commerce in the said product is injuriously affected by the lack of a local board to regulate such product, at any time propose a scheme for the marketing of such product, and the governor in council may approve of such scheme and authorize the board to administer such scheme directly or through any agency which it may establish. Such scheme shall continue in force until terminated by the governor in council.
12. (1) The governor in council may, by order or regulation published in the Canada Gazette, restrict the importation into Canada of any natural product which enters Canada in competition with a regulated product, and the governor in council shall have power to make regulations to provide for the licensing by the minister of importers, or otherwise to enforce any order made hereunder.
(2)	The governor in council may, by order or regulation published in the Canada Gazette,-
(a)	provide that any natural product shall not be exported from Canada without a licence;
(b)	prescribe the forms of such licences, the terms and condit:ons thereof and the persons who shall have authority to issue the same;
(c)	impose penalties for breach of any such order or regulation or of any licence issued thereunder, and, generally, make such provision or authorize the doing of such acts or things as may in his discretion be deemed necessary or expedient for giving full effect to any orders, regulations or licences made or issued hereunder.
Then I refer to section 14:
14. Every person who fails to comply with any order or determination of the board or of a local board or any regulation of the governor in council shall be guilty of an offence and punishable on summary conviction with a fine of not less than twenty-five dollars and not more than five hundred dollars, or to imprisonment not exceeding three months, or to both fine and imprisonment.
In part 2, which deals with investigations, it will be found that very similar powers are given to bodies as yet undetermined. I submit that the reading of these sections leaves no doubt whatever that the principles underlying this measure are first that of limiting production, second that of restricting trade and third doing both these things by creating monopolies with regard to certain products that are

to be marketed. And fourth, all this is to be done, not by an act of this parliament which will leave the matter in a known and finally determined condition when the bill is signed by the representative of the crown and becomes law but by giving these powers to bodies that are still to be brought into existence and giving to the governor in council, rather than having held within the control of this parliament, the power to restrict both imports and exports and the control of all expenditures under the act. Our position, Mr. Speaker, is that we are wholly favourable to the regulation of trade to improve marketing conditions, but that the regulation and marketing should be by act of this parliament in accordance with parliamentary procedure and practice and not by bodies other than parliament itself.
In conclusion may I by way of illustrating what I have in mind direct attention to the amendment that was moved on the second reading of the Unemployment and Farm Relief Continuance Act, Bill No. 24, which amendment came before the house on March 30, 1932, and which Your Honour permitted to remain before the house and to be voted upon as entirely in order. I submit that the present amendment as regards the points at issue, is on all fours with that amendment, which was moved by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) and seconded by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston). The name of the bill was Unemployment and Farm Relief, that was its purpose. The amendment, which was directed not at its purpose, or name, but at the principles upon which it was based, was as follows:
That this bill be not now read a second time but that it be resolved:
1.	That this house has been from the commencement of the session and continues to be ready and willing to consider and vote without delay any money or grant, submitted and asked for by the government for relieving distress and providing employment throughout Canada.
2.	That this house cannot surrender the rights of the people of Canada, through their representatives in parliament, to maintain direct control over matters of taxation and expenditure, nor vest in the governor in council or in any other body absolute and despotic powers under the guise of dealing with peace, order and good government, particularly while parliament is in session.
I repeat that as regards the points involved in this discussion the amendment now before the house in regard to this marketing act is on all fours with the amendment which was held to be in order in 1932.

The minister may from time to time make regulations:-

regulations

I would like to point out that it has been the custom from time immemorial to discuss the principle of a bill on the second reading to enable members to express their views and if so desired to change the form of a proposal which is made to the house. The same rule applies to all amendments. When a motion is made by a member and put to the house by the speaker, it is the right of any other member to move to amend it in accordance

with certain rules. Members may not be willing to adopt the question as proposed to them and may consequently desire to modify it in various ways. When we are voting on the supply bill, we very often preface the amendment by saying that while the house is willing to vote supply to His Majesty to carry on the public business, we object to such and such an expenditure. Bourinot at page 509 states:
The second reading of a bill is that stage when it is proper to enter into a discussion and propose a motion relative to the principle of the measure. The Senate has a rule on the subject:
"64. The principle of a bill is usually debated at its second reading."
The commons have no rule on the subject, but the practice of the house is always to discuss the principle of a bill at this stage. Any member may propose as an amendment a resolution declaratory of some principle adverse to, or differing from, the principles, policy or provisions of the bill.
We may favour a marketing board on certain conditions, a marketing board whose expenditures, whose cost to the country, would be controlled by parliament. It having been moved that Bill No. 51, an act to improve the methods and practices involved in the marketing of natural products in Canada and in export trade, and to make further provision in connection therewith, be now read the second time, the Right Hon. Mr. Mackenzie King moved in amendment that all the words after the first word "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
This house, while prepared to support legislation for assisting the orderly marketing of natural products, is unalterably opposed to the enactment of any compulsory measure which delegates to unnamed and undetermined individuals, groups or organizations, sweeping powers over the production and trade and commerce of the nation, and which confers upon a minister of the crown and upon the governor in council unprecedented authority and unusual powers to restrict production, and interprovincial, inter-imperial and foreign trade as regards both exports and imports, as well as other autocratic powers.
The Hon. Mr. Stevens raised the point of order as to whether the said amendment is in order inasmuch as it constitutes what might be termed a declaration of policy instead of
offering reasons why consideration of the bill should not be proceeded with or should be postponed, or proposing something else germane to the actual motion before the house.
The Right Hon. Mr. Mackenzie King in moving the amendment quoted paragraph 755 of Beauehesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms-which paragraph is published as a quotation from May, thirteenth edition, page 390, and is repeated by Bourinot at page 509- as follows:
It is also competent to a member who desires to place on record any special reasons for not agreeing to the second reading of a bill, to move as an amendment to the question, a resolution declaratory of some principle adverse to, or differing from, the principles, policy or provisions of the bill, . . .
This rule is subject to certain limitations. If the right hon. member had continued to quote from May, he would have found the following reference to an amendment to a motion for second reading of a bill:
Nor may such an amendment deal with the provisions of the bill upon which it is moved, nor anticipate amendments thereto which may be moved in committee. '
(May, thirteenth edition, page 391.)
The precedent cited in May in support of this is found in 188 Parliamentry Debates, fourth series, column 76, The Education (Scotland) Bill:
Mr. Speaker: I have to rule that the amendment standing in the name of the hon. member for Glasgow and Aberdeen universities-to the effect that the house while welcoming educational legislation for Scotland regrets that the present measure does not propose change in the educational areas which is urgently required in the interests of efficient administration-is not technically in order, because it does not challenge the principle of the bill. The question raised can be decided by an amendment to the bill itself. If the hon. member wants to object to the second reading, he should move that the bill be read this day six months.
The amendment moved by the right hon. leader of the opposition does not challenge the principle of Bill No. 51, and it anticipates the committee stage. It declares that the "house is prepared to support legislation for assisting the orderly marketing of natural products," and the bill is intituled "an act to improve the methods and practices of marketing of natural products." There is so much similarity between those two propositions that one cannot be moved as a resaon to reject the second reading of a bill enunciating the other.
The amendment further declares that the house is unalterably opposed to the granting of certain powers and the application of certain methods in the giving of government assistance to the marketing of natural pro-

ducts, but does not connect the granting of those powers or the application of those methods with the bill. It does not declare any principle adverse to or differing from the principle, policy or provisions of the bill. The bill deals with powers and methods which may be altered in committee.
The objection .to the enactment of any compulsory measure which delegates to unnamed and undetermined individuals, groups or organizations, sweeping powers over the production and trade and commerce of the nation can be dealt with by amendments when the committee of the whole is considering section 3 of the bill which establishes the dominion marketing board, and section 4 which defines the powers of the board. The action to be taken by the governor in council and the minister in administering the act is described in almost every section of the bill and may be strengthened or weakened by amendment when the bill is in committee.
The case cited by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth differs from this case. There a definite declaration as to what the mover was in favour of was laid down; in this case the amendment declares as to what enactments the mover is opposed to, without connecting them with the bill or the principle of the bill.
The objections raised in the proposed amendment cannot be looked upon as reasons why Bill No. 51 should not now be proceeded with and, moreover, they may be considered after the bill has been read a second time. For these reasons I find the proposed amendment to be out of order.

Mr. Speaker, this marketing bill which I hold in my hand is one of the greatest compounds of good, bad and indifferent that it has fallen to my lot to analyze and decide upon. So much is that the case that at times and in places the bad features of this bill seem almost to supersede the good. Notwithstanding that, however, and having regard to the fact that I hope we will have two opportunities before two committees to expunge the bad features and preserve the good ones I have decided to support the second reading of the bill. That is my best judgment. At this stage, and before giving my reasons for so doing, I should like to read an extract from Hansard of May 13, 1932, in which I gave expression to these words:
I think we have reached a time in our history when agriculture is simply staggering to its fall, and we can afford to ease up a little in our extreme political alignments and work on behalf of agriculture even if we have to work through a Tory government, which is the only avenue available at this time. That is pretty straight talk, but that is the way I feel. I am in opposition now; there are not enough of us here to perform the functions of government. The electors, in their wisdom, elected another government and we have a new minister of agriculture. I have not very long to assist agriculture now, perhaps ten or fifteen years more, and I am prepared to work through this government until the electors provide us with a better avenue. Things are so bad in connection with agriculture that I believe I would work through Beelzebub himself if necessary, and therefore much more through the minister. Conditions are so distressing on many farms that we cannot afford to quibble as to where the good things may come from at this time.
That is exactly the way I still feel, and I am thinking not of the government or even of parliament but of the farmers and producers throughout Canada who asked for this legislation.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: For this legislation?

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
What they think this legislation is. Having made the merits and demerits of the bill the basis of my decision I think it is up to me to mention some of the good features of the bill, and I think it has good features. In passing I might say,

Mr. Speaker, that I think the bill contains more than one principle, and that is the difficulty we have been up against. There are many principles involved, but to me the outstanding point is that a long deferred marketing act has been presented to us, and I have to decide what I am going to do with it. My decision is to support the second reading of the bill and, before the agriculture committee, where I hope it will go, to expurgate the bad features and "hold fast to that which is good." I believe it is quite safe ground when I take that attitude. We have then a marketing bill-and may I say that we are the last part of this British Empire to have such legislation. All the dominions, with the exception of Canada, have a marketing act. I do not say that that in itself is sufficient argument in favour of accepting any bill; as a matter of fact I believe in the principle of standing alone for the right, if you have to. But it is worth while to think about that feature, namely that we are the last part of the British Empire to pass such legislation. As a matter of fact we will soon be the tail end of creation with respect to marketing legislation, because more than thirty other countries have it. That is also worth thinking about.
We have before us a marketing bill, and I believe in part of it as at present drafted, but the bill which I hope will go forward from this house after we have concluded our deliberations I hope to be able to support almost in toto. I believe, further, in a marketing board. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, the government to which I belonged is responsible for a wheat marketing board act. In connection with the wheat board we were successful in ou.r methods of reconciling the jurisdiction of the dominion with that of the provinces. The legislation in this connection was passed in the year 1922, and to it some rather unfair references were made by the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Turnbull). However, we shall not go into that matter now. The method of passing enabling legislation and concurring legislation is laid down in this bill, and was laid down twelve years ago by the government to which I had the honour of belonging. At that time the same principle of enabling legislation was involved. Of course, we did not deal with the same objectionable details, but we did have to deal with the same constitutional difficulties as are herein dealt with in this marketing act. The province of British Columbia established a satisfactory system of marketing boards, but in that province they always ran up against the final difficulty of

Marketing Act-Mr. Motherwell
standing the test in the courts, and without this legislation they were unable to carry out their marketing programs.
I have given three reasons why I like this measure. Then we come to a feature of the bill to which a great many people have taken strong objection. Owing to the paucity of information given by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) in his speech one cannot wonder at such objections. I am sorry to have to make that statement. Of course, the minister w'as labouring under this tremendous difficulty, namely, that when he proposed the second reading of the bill the recesses and rafters of this building were reverberating witih the Liberal cheers of victory from South Oxford. At that moment my good friend the minister was put into the front line trenches to explain this bill. Under those circumstances I think the enthusiasm would have been taken out of anyone, I do not care how young or old a political warrior he might be. However, I have no brief for my hon. friend, nor do I intend to make excuses for him. The fact remains however that in view of the meagreness of the information he gave the house I am not surprised that the opposition of many hon. gentlemen was invited. I did not know then what many of the features of this bill meant and I do not know yet.
Then, we find the provision prohibiting the export of certain unnamed commodities. Is it any wonder, without any knowledge of what is meant, there has been strong opposition to this also. That is a provision we should have had long ago, a provision at least some portion of which we have already exercised. It would prohibit low grade commodities, such as low grade live stock, low grade wheat or, in fact, low grade anything being shipped to the export markets of the world. The Antipodes have had that legislation for I don't know how many years. Denmark has it. They export the good and leave the bad at home, or do something else with it. When one understands this provision he realizes that instead of it being an objection to the bill it is a virtue.
At the present time we have a congested European and British wheat market. Would it not be the part of wisdom at this time when there is justification for it, to tell those who have low grade wheat, say No. 6, that it is not fair to send such wheat to a market already congested and thereby pull down the value of the higher grades. That is not a wise procedure. This is the time to say, I repeat, that the low grades should not be placed on already congested markets, thereby in some measure lessening the opportunities afforded for sale of the higher grades.
Especially is that true when there is an opening for the same low grade wheat in the Orient, if there is another opening for wheat anywhere at the present time. As every hon. member knows, the only way to compete in the orient is by offering low grade wheat at prices in competition with rice. I do not know whether the government understands this situation as do some other hon. members, but certainly they have not explained it. For thitf reason I am not surprised that this particular feature of the bill has met with strong opposition. However, having had conversations with some of the staff in the Department of Agriculture, and being in a position to guess the rest of it, I have assumed-and I believe I am right in my assumption-that this provision is for the purpose of meeting such situations as we now' have whereby low grade commodities are authorized to be kept off congested markets. That is good practice. I may state frankly, Mr. Speaker, that the late government did, without any of this legislation, refuse the shipment abroad of poor live stock. We had no legislation to support us, but we just took chances, when exporting cattle to Great Britain shortly after the major portions of the embargo were removed in 1923. We did take the responsibility at Montreal and at other ports for saying that certain low grade cattle could not take ship. No one objected. We just took it for granted that we had that authority. Possibly that may not have been the right procedure for us to adopt, but may I say it did keep low grade animals off the British market, and that is what this legislation proposes to do legally.

I do not think we had. We were simply assuming that it was the sensible thing to do and, acting sanely in the matter, we prevented such low grade stock from going anyway.
I now turn to the section which has to do with the storing and preserving of farm commodities. I am bound to take the stand that I would have gone even farther in this connection. I should like to have seen the processing of commodities included, a procedure which would have my support. If processing were included the board would have the

Marketing Act-Mr. Motherwell
right to establish somewhere in Canada a demonstration packing plant, without which we will never get to the farmer the information he must have in order to secure his confidence in our packing plants. This principle was demonstrated in connection with terminal elevators. Do you ever hear any cry about the terminal elevator now? No, because the government established one. May I say it was not our government, but the government of my hon. friends opposite. Although I do not think it is always a paying concern, I do believe it established the fact that there were not in connection with the terminal elevators the abuses that many had believed. Since that action was taken there has been no difficulty. Therefore I say that if processing were added, the proper authority would have the right to establish an experimental abattoir which would show the farmers just what profits were being made and could be made or not be made in the matter of processing live stock. I believe one such abattoir would be sufficient, and that it should be placed in the stock yards auction market and not away from the yards. It should be favourably situated in a position convenient to the animals. I have outlined six good features in this legislation. It would be sufficient to take those six favorable features as a nucleus for the bill and while adding others thereto try to eliminate the really bad ones- and I tell you they are here in abundance as the bill now stands.
Then, some people shy at the bill because it is said to represent state socialism. Well, as I understand the dictum and policies of our friends to the left, the C.C.F., it is that which they have preached in this house on many occasions, namely, the doctrine of "production for use and not for profit." Why, Mr. Speaker, the avowed purpose of this bill is to make more profits, and if my friends of the C.C.F. believe in "production for use and not for profit," they should oppose this bill because avowedly it is out for more profits for the producers, and it is because of that, that I am supporting it. So this bill does not present any feature of state socialism in that respect.
State socialism also implies and declares for a change in ownership. Is there any change of ownership even remotely implied in this bill? Not at all. This bill however is a piece of social legislation gone to excess in the matter of control, gone to folly, and that is what is causing so much opposition. My hon. friends opposite are not familiar with this class of legislation, and they seem to think that the farther they go the better. Did you ever hear the saying, that too far east is west?

Did you ever hear about Paddy's chimney being so plumb that it was over plumb, or did you ever hear of a man walking so straight that he leaned over backwards? Now the government in their anxiety to have a wonderful bill, different from any other bill they ever knew of, made this bill reach out to all creation and include not only farm products but nearly all the natural resources of the nation. Anybody who knew anything about reforms would not act in that way, because it can only invite opposition and disaster.
I do not want to refer unnecessarily to the former government's policy of standardizing various farm products, but what would have happened if we in one bill had attempted to standardize all at once all the farm products that we finally succeeded in standardizing at the end of nine years of effort? If we had put the whole of that in one bill, we would not have got to first base with it, but by bringing about measures of grading gradually, and familiarizing the house and the country with the policy of standardization, we finally consummated that policy at the expiry of our term of office.
I have given some of the reason why this bill is not state socialism. I shall be interested to hear my C.C.F. friends, who are supporting this bill on the ground that it is state socialism, reconcile such support with their doctrine of "production for use, and not for profit."
I have many reservations regarding many of the features of this bill, and I must say that unless some of these features are eliminated or substantially altered during the committee stage I shall be obliged to vote against the bill in committee and on the third reading, but if these objectionable features are eliminated or substantially removed, if the bill is expurgated, and cleansed of these bad features, I shall continue to support it through to the end.
The bill is too comprehensive to start with. Why experiment on such a ghastly big scale? Is it wise to include all these commodities to which the bill refers? Every new commodity outside agriculture that you are going to control by this bill only creates further opposition to the measure. Why not start out with a limited number of commodities where control is likely to be supported strongly by the community in which it is started In many of the communities control is already under way in regard to some commodities, and the only difficulty is that they run up against the decisions of the privy council.

Not under the enabling legislation. We had some experience in the Department of Agriculture with regard to live stock and live stock products in that respect. One of the first duties I performed on coming to Ottawa was to write to every one of the provinces sending them a copy of our proposed legislation with respect to live stock and live stock products, and asking them if they could see their way to passing enabling or concurrent legislation as the case might be, and after four or five years every one of the provinces did. So we had that principle recognized in the department in connection with the grading of hogs, the grading of eggs, and the control of stock yards. Any legal difficulties in the way were removed by enabling legislation.
I think it is also a big mistake not to mention in the bill who is going to administer the law. We have the Minister of Agriculture sponsoring the bill, and this is supposed to be a marketing act for agricultural products mainly, but as a matter of fact the door has been thrown so wide open that it deals with the products of our fisheries, of the forest and what not, and three or four ministers might well claim the right to administer the act. It is true that the preponderating feature of the bill is agricultural, but nevertheless there are many other commodities dealt with, and knowing the ambition and the flair which the Minister of Trade and Commerce seems to have for agriculture, and not knowing in the bill who is going to administer this act, on that ground alone I would oppose it if I thought that any other minister than the Minister of Agriculture would be in charge of it.
Then we have the wide open interpretation of "natural products." Just imagine all that that includes! My right hon. leader and other members on this side have not misinterpreted the bill in its definition of "natural products." It includes almost every natural product and products processed therefrom under the sun. Did hon. gentlemen see Mr. Taschereau's interpretation in this morning's paper? There are all kinds of possibilities of difficulty and danger associated with grabbing the whole practically of our natural resources and putting them all into this one bill that is supposed to be primarily for agriculture. It really looks as if a lot of kindergarten legislators were in charge of this measure and are endeavouring to bring within one act what nobody ever saw the like of previously-practically the whole natural production of this country.
Nevertheless, I believe still that we can make a good act of it. Let the Minister of Agriculture take this bill to the agriculture
committee as he has done with similar bills. Bills of this nature have always been sent to the agriculture committee, unless it was simply a matter of making sosie trifling correction or something like that. As a matter of fact, last week the Minister of Trade and Commerce referred to the standing committee on agriculture a bill that was not one-hundredth so important as this. I certainly disagree with this amendment to the grain act as it stands, but as it was going to be sent to the agriculture committee I agreed to it with such reservations as I am now making to this marketing bill.
I wonder if I might get the Prime Minister's attention for one minute.

My hon. friend
does not know what he is talking about. It was always the policy of the former government to refer agricultural bills to the agriculture committee and to bring about reforms gradually. Practical reformers invariably start with something that you can handle, to avoid running into difficulties and disaster

Marketing Act-Mr. Motherwell
by having too ambitious a plan and spoiling the whole lot-in other words, creep before attempting to walk. That is my suggestion to the government. It will not cost anything, and they do not need to follow it.
Under the provisions of this bill wheat is included, and that is sufficient to make me oppose the bill. The situation in the west has been fierce since some tried to bring about a hundred per cent pool. If that is being considered as desirable the government will be simply putting the fat into the fire. The controversy is dying out, so why stir it up at this stage? This commodity should not be included in the bill at present, in my estimation. I am willing to take my chance when I make the statement I do in connection with this highly controversial problem, which should not be stirred afresh now. My proposal would be to start out with say milk and its products, fruit and its products, bacon, cattle, honey, maple sugar, perhaps a dozen or so all told, in connection with some of which marketing schemes are already under way. All that would be necessary would be to provide the necessary legislative machinery and put it in motion, and the government would be on safe constitutional and democratic ground. There would thus be the minimum chances of opposition and subsequent failure. Ten or twelve commodities could be mentioned and then the words "and such other commodities as may be added thereto from time to time by parliament."

speechtext: Perhaps the hon. gentleman is aware that it is a matter of legal construction that it is far more desirable to use a general term than to endeavour to specify. All the branches of an industry would be included in the declaration of the industry, so therefore there is no purpose in that argument.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
We have the same provision now in connection with the weed acts of the west. Those acts state that noxious weeds are so and so and so and so, naming the kinds, and such other weeds as may be added thereto from time to time. Lawyers always place great value on precedent, and I am giving one to the Prime Minister. Even if there were no precedent, I think my suggestion is quite sensible. It would be safety first anyway.
There is another section of the bill which is open to justifiable criticism. It reads:
The board shall consist of such number of persons as the governor in council may from time to time determine, and each member shall hold office during pleasure-

There is a general rumour that this board will consist largely of departmental officials. As far as I am concerned, I am willing to accept these officials without any reservation but everyone does not know them as I do. The government will be open to the charge of establishing a centralized bureaucracy. "Let not your good be evil spoken of," is good advice. No one is so perfect and above suspicion that he can afford to place himself under suspicion. Why not state that the members of this board shall be say the deputy minister of agriculture, the director of farm economics, the dairy commissioner or such other officials as the government may choose? The same principle is employed in appointing many members of the grain standards board. There should also be on this board a practical farmer who also knows the technique of agriculture. There should also be one more member. What about the consumer? Great Britain has taken every precaution on behalf of the consumer. The government is turning loose a lot of boards and giving them unprecedented powers and is making no provision to protect the consumer. I realize the consumer quite often is a doubting man who frequently disbelieves that anyone is thinking of him very much. He does not seem to care a great deal, even at election time. Some of them were quite willing in 1930 to pay more for their butter and then paid less. However that may be, I suggest that on this board there should be a representative business man, one who knows the needs of the consumer. The government should not assume that the producers will be always so comprehensive in their outlook that they will think of the consumer's viewpoint at all times. I believe that this board would be greatly improved if all interests were represented thereon, but the government has the power and it can do just as it pleases. This would be a step to disarming the criticism that this is bureaucracy; it would be a board upon which everyone was represented, including the consumer. I am sure that such a board would appeal to the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young). I believe it would appeal to all sensible people and if it were submitted at any public meeting it would receive approval, I think.
Subsection 7 of section 4 has been discussed, and apparently this has to do with quotas. When we make provisions for quotas against commodities coming in from Great Britain, they will say, we are accommodatingly inviting the establishing of quotas by that country against Canada. By means of a gentlemen's agreement with this government, Great Britain has put into force a quota against our cattle and there is talk of quotas

Marketing Act-Mr. Motherwell
against our oats, dairy products and other commodities. This would simply be an invitation to Major Elliot, the British Minister of Agriculture, to put on further quotas against Canada. Provision is being made also for reprisal quotas on our goods by foreign countries. This looks bad to me and I should like to know more about it in committee. I may be wrong in this, but that is my understanding of the clause. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) just whispered the word " quota " in his speech. I do not believe there were half a dozen members who heard what he said. Quotas are not mentioned in the bill but yet they are snuggled and smuggled in in a confusion of words and terms. The government has launched this bill without proper explanation and is amazed when it receives opposition. I am amazed that I do not oppose it myself, but my love of some of the things that are in the bill is greater than my dislike for some of the objectionable things. I hope the government will reconsider its decision and send this bill to the agriculture committee where the winnowing takes place.
Nothing is said in the bill as to the percentage of vote which shall determine the action to be taken by the minister. The government is pretending to follow the British act but this bill does not hint as to what size of vote will be necessary to launch a marketing project. What is it to be? Is it to be a straight majority? Any one of us is glad to get here on a straight majority of two or three, and I have even known hon. members who have been permitted to sit in this house by the vote cast by the returning officer. But these marketing matters are looked upon differently; there should be somewhere between a 66 to 75 per cent favourable vote before these marketing proposals go into force. There is no hint of what it is going to be so long as the minister is satisfied. Let me appeal to him. He should not put himself into that position. Let him consider the immense responsibility he is assuming of being the only determining factor with nothing to guide him but his own judgment and that of his staff in regard to so important a matter. Even assuming they will be absolutely right, how will the great body of the people be convinced that that is the right way to carry out that plan? That is not the proper way to deal with the matter. The British act places the majority at 66 per cent. May I say there again the Department of Agriculture has been determining policies on a two-thirds vote in connection with slaughtering animals for tuberculosis. Before a restricted area can be established, you have to get the consent of 66 per cent of the stock owners
of that district. On that 66 per cent basis the government staff in the health of animals branch, after providing for all the preliminaries in connection with the matter, go out with inspectors, organize a veterinary crew in the affected area, test out the reactors, kill them and salvage them at the nearest abattoir. Will the other third agree to that? They do agree with very few exceptions. It is common sense that they should. The interest of the whole is greater than that of a part,-a third. That is being proposed by me in connection with some features of this bill with even more favourable modifications.
Another proposal I would make-and I feel my leader is absolutely right in regard to it- is that until the board builds up public confidence in itself these marketing proposals should in the interests of everybody be submitted to parliament After parliament sees that the board are using their powers wisely and well in the interests of those whom we are all desirous of serving, that is the producers, then the necessity of coming to parliament could be discontinued after, say two or three years. Parliament is giving the Minister of Agriculture greater powers in his recent bills than it did to the last Minister of Agriculture, and to the last minister parliament gave infinitely greater powers than it did to his predecessor. How do we account for that? It is because the various ministers administered their standardization legislation in conjunction with the various producers' organizations concerned and gave constantly growing satisfaction. I know some producers will raise the objection: Oh, we shall have to lose another year if we have to come to parliament for its approval of a marketing project. We can avoid losing another year in connection with this scheme in this way for this year. Let us get this bill through the committee on agriculture as quickly as possible; let us get it through the commitee of the whole also as quickly as possible, then through the senate and royal assent. If I know anything about the matter, we are likely to be here until the middle of July. Before that date one or more marketing schemes can, I feel, be got ready for submission to parliament for approval, as they are now already under way. I know how impatient farmers are in regard to getting any reforms that they may already have been waiting years for. It is far better to make sure of one's ground and then go ahead rather than to be precipitate in one's action and find it necessary to retrace one's steps. That is a proposal, I think, worth while considering and after a year or two or even three years parliament would have no hesitation in saying:



Marketing Act-Mr. Motherwell
All right; so long as you are conducting this business the way you are doing, we will let you go ahead with your new marketing proposals, always reserving the right to withdraw that power from you if you abuse it.
The clause with regard to the right to restrict imports was brought up by a number of speakers on this side. That may mean quotas; it may be aggravating regulations or it may be tariffs; I do not care what it is, we have no right as a parliament to delegate power to local boards to control imports. I believe in delegating powers where that is warranted, to producers as is now done to the legal profession, to what we call the learned profession, to which is delegated powers and remarkable administrative powers too. We have the same authority and right to delegate powers to farmer groups or marketing bodies. But there is a point to which I do not think we should go and that is to delegate the control of imports. That control is something that should surely belong to parliament. Let us not fall over ourselves trying to be good to the farmers as it is not really being good to them when we go this extreme length. The farmers who asked for this legislation do not approve of a great deal of the stuff in this bill; they are not particularly concerned so long as they have in it what they want; the bad things do not interest them much. They are all wondering why we are objecting to the bad things. It is our duty to protest against the bad features, to protect the people who are asking for this legislation from the consequences of the government's proposed actions, and to eliminate the bad features so that we can go out to the country and defend all the features of the bill. I would like this bill to go out to the country as the product, not of the Conservatives alone but of the whole parliament of Canada, and then it would be launched without any bias or bigotry. I have had experience in these matters; I have met not with this kind of opposition but with direct opposition from almost every manjack on the other side in connection with our standardization proposals; in regard to hog and egg grading particularly, with the result that nearly every Tory in the country was opposed to the legislation and greatly hampered the acceptance of it throughout the country. This parliament, from all sides, should get reasonably behind the measure. Let us work out the best bill we can, get it started along the line of least resistance, get our noses through the door jamb first, then our heads and shoulders, then our whole bodies, and we shall find the confidence of the country will go out towards this proposal and all hands will be for it. Some

may say that is an ideal not attainable, although I believe it is. May I point out that this is not a vision; It is not a case of either young men seeing visions or old men dreaming dreams. In this parliament in connection with the grain act in 1929 and 1930, we worked out in the committee on agriculture and the subcommittee a solution that has stood the test of time ever since, and to which we gave one hundred per cent approval.
