This is a most important piece of legislation and we should hesitate before we pass it. I think that particular feature of it is going a little too far. Like other hon. members I too have received representations with respect to this measure.
I feel, however, I am fairly accurate when I say that this bill is not altogether what our cooperative organizations want, and in my judgment it is likely in the long run to do them more harm than good. It is certainly going to interfere with their own initiative in carrying on their activities. I cannot see how parliament can afford to delegate its power and authority to an independent board and still have the members of this house function as they properly should. I am not a very old member of the commons, but I have vision enough to think we should have some control over the different bodies that are set up by this institution and I am not as yet prepared to delegate the authority of parliament to some outside body, if for no other reason than that if this delegation of authority continues for a little longer the people might think parliament unnecessary and I might be deprived of my position.
I repeat-and I want to make this abundantly clear-that I am absolutely in sympathy with the cooperative movements of this country and I think they should be assisted in every legitimately possible way, but I hope people will realize that there is some responsibility on the part of members of parliament in dealing with these different matters. This bill, in my opinion, is not a marketing bill at all; that is altogether a wrong conception of it; it would be more rightly called a regulating measure. May I submit with all deference that the various objects the bill attempts to carry out in the way of grading and standardization of natural products can be and are being carried out

very largely under legislation provided with respect to those different products. This year we have passed amendments to the Dairy Produce Act, the Fruit Act and some other acts under which we dealt with these very matters, so that in connection with them I do not think the bill is necessary.
Another weakness in the bill is that it fails to indicate where the board would be directed to extend any of its efforts toward promoting trade or getting markets. That is something that should have been in the bill as a duty of the dominion marketing board, and it is not there. In this regard I should like to refer to a matter with which the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Totzke) dealt. We saw the other day in the press a communication from the wheat conference indicating that France had asked, if she restricted her acreage in wheat or the assistance to her own growers, what she could expect in return from other countries. The committee, quite properly, I think, said they could not promise anything, as that was the responsibility of the respective governments. The point I wish to make is this: France having made that statement, which we have no reason to think was not made in perfect good faith, what are we going to do to meet her? Is this marketing board to be clothed with power to deal with matters of that kind? There is no indication of it in the bill. The bill, however, does make it abundantly clear that if the situation were reversed and France were under agreement delivering goods to this country, this board could take steps by way of regulation to curtail the importation of such goods. That seems clear under section 12.
I submit that before this bill was presented and the house asked to deal with it we were entitled to have and should have had the advantage of the findings of the committee investigating mass buying and price spreads. If the minister can explain why that course was not pursued and this bill delayed until the report of that committee was more nearly ready, I should appreciate it. Personally I should like to see this bill referred to a special committee or a select standing committee of the house so that witnesses could be called to speak for the people interested-

In rising at this time to say a few words concerning this marketing bill I assure you, sir, that it is with no desire to prolong the debate, which to my mind has already been too long. Session after session for the last three or four years, hon. members opposite have filled page after page of Hansard in putting before the house the lamentable condition in which the farmers of Canada found themselves. This lamentation relates largely to western Canada; it does not apply with equal force to the farmers of eastern Canada. I have the greatest sympathy with the farmers of the west. I visited their country last August, and what I saw in some of the western provinces made me feel very glad indeed that I lived just as far east as I could possibly get without getting my feet wet. I do not say this in any light way; I am a farmer myself, and perhaps no man sitting in this house who is not a farmer realizes fully what it means for a farmer to go out in the spring, prepare his soil, sow his seed, put in long hours of labour with high hope in his heart, and then when the autumn comes find that he has absolutely nothing to reap. Let me say in passing that no matter what measures may come before the house at this session for the purpose of alleviating the sufferings of my brother farmers in the southern portions of the three prairie provinces, I would vote for them cheerfully and willingly and give them my most hearty and loyal support.
As I was saying, for the past three or four years hon. members opposite have dwelt upon the condition of the farmer's of Canada, and then they jauntily ask, "What are you doing about it? What are you going to do? Why don't you bring down some policy to alleviate their sufferings and improve their condition?" They have said so much along that line that the farmers of Canada are looking to us to do something. Now when the government brings down a bill that has been carefully considered, not by the minister and the Department of Agriculture alone but by agricultural organizations and societies all over Canada, they having given their advice to the minister on the matter on many occasions, what do we hear from hon. gentlemen opposite? It appears that they are afraid now that this government are really going to do something to better the condition of the farmer. That is what I gather from the very stiff opposition that is being put up against this measure.
I am not sure what the effects of the measures embodied in this bill may be. No
man is sure, not even the minister himself. But I will say this: the bill is at least an honest effort to make it possible so to regulate the marketing of the products of the farm that the spread between what the producer who toils in the fields gets for his product, and what the consumer in the towns and the cities pays for it, is subject to control. This bill is an attempt to bring those two figures a little closer together, so that the producer may get a fair and equitable share of the consumer's dollar and the consumer at the other end shall not be exploited.
The hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Weir), who has just taken his seat, raised the objection that the bill is premature, that we should have waited until the price spreads committee which is now carrying on its investigations had completed its activities and brought in its report. My answer is that days and days ago enough evidence had already been brought out in that committee to justify the adoption of this bill. Then the hon. member said that the minister in introducing the bill did not give a sufficient explanation of the way it would work out and the final results to be expected. The minister, I take it, gave all the explanation he could give. It must be borne in mind that this bill merely sets up a central marketing board, but the working out of the bill, in other words the bill itself, cannot come into operation or be effective until enabling legislation has been passed by the different legislatures throughout the dominion. Further than that, the legislation that may be passed by the different legislatures cannot itself become operative until the producers of a specific product get together and say to themselves, "We want to take advantage of the provisions of this bill." That is the way the bill will operate, and the local marketing boards that will be set up in the various provinces, and the primary producers of these products themselves, will I take it have more to do with the regulations governing the operation of this bill than will the Minister of Agriculture himself. That is a strong statement to make; I know it is a strong statement, but I believe in my heart that it is correct.
The hon. member for Macdonald also laboured the point very heavily that this bill was aimed at cooperative organization. To my mind nothing is further from the fact. It is true, as the minister pointed out, and as other members of the house who have spoken on this question have pointed out, that these cooperative organizations have not always been one hundred per cent successful. Their intention was right; the object for which they were organized was right; but often those who

Marketing Act

Mr. Myers
were placed in charge of them lacked experience in the business that they were called upon to undertake.
I am a farmer myself and I know our ways, our faults, our peculiarities and our failings. I have attended a great many meetings in my time leading up to cooperation on the part of the farmers and I have not one word to say against it, remember that. But I have often noticed that some chap-might I be permitted to call him a smart Aleck-who knew a lot less about farming than about talking and putting out ideas, was sometimes responsible for getting the farmers together. He would say, "Boys, let us have a meeting in the hall a week from to-night and we will talk about marketing eggs, or poultry or potatoes or some other commodity." So the farmers meet there. This chap is usually chairman and secretary and spokesman, and as a result a number of motions are made And resolutions passed and they come away with a cooperative organization established, and this chap who knows absolutely nothing about the business, about establishing trade connections in foreign countries or in other provinces, finds himself suddenly at the head of an organization about which he knows very little. Yet, let me repeat, we have throughout Canada a number of fine cooperative organizations that are functioning very well, and this bill is by no means intended to interfere with their activities. In fact, I can see where it will be of great advantage to cooperative organizations of this kind. Take for instance in our own province, and I speak of that province because I know it best; we have a number of cooperative organizations known as marketing clubs for the marketing of our hogs. We have a number of them throughout our little province. Under the provisions of this bill, instead of doing away with these local marketing boards, we would centralize them together in one, and they as one cooperative marketing organization could operate under the provisions of this measure.
The hon. member for Macdonald, in closing his remarks, said he feared that this bill was nothing more or less than a setting up of the quota system in Canada and the application of quotas to the marketing or exporting of Canadian farm products. With all due respect to the hon. member, and I know that he is a gentleman of great ability, may I say that he seems to put the cart before the horse. As I take it, countries do not set up quotas for the purpose of exporting their own goods, but they do set up quotas to regulate the import of goods into their own territory; and it is that

angle of the question that we in Canada may have to deal with in the near future. In other words, we with our products, seeking to get into outside markets, shall have to meet the quotas that are established in the different countries with which we have to trade.
The hon. member-and I might as well finish dealing with his remarks first-saw something in section 12 of this bill, and it was pretty much the same bogy that was raised by his right hon. leader-that old question of parliament renouncing its rights and passing them over to order in council. He read section 12 of the bill which provides:	,
The governor in council may, by order or regulation published in the Canada Gazette, restrict the importation into Canada of any natural product . . .
And so forth. Has the hon. gentleman forgotten that for the past four years that very clause, embodied in other acts, used in the same way but in other lines, has been the greatest safeguard that the dairy industry of Canada has ever enjoyed? Does he not know that we dairymen of Canada are protected against the undue importation of New Zealand butter by regulations and orders in council? Has he any fault to find with that? I fancy that if he had taken time to think that matter over he might well have left that part of his address unsaid. Then he concluded his remarks by saying that this bill is not a marketing bill at all, and he followed other members on the opposite side of the house who have taken serious objection to the bill all the way through. They have criticized it, even the title, clause by clause, section by section. But I have yet to hear one single member of them get up and read a better bill. I have yet to hear a single one of them get up and from his place announce something that is better. Their attitude is this, "We will object to this bill: we will do our best to pull it to pieces, to tear it down, but we are not building up anything better to take its place".
I want to tell hon. gentlemen opposite that the farmers of Canada are to-day watching them very closely and very narrowly. Newspapers circulate into every home; radios are operated every night. Hon. members must know that the radio is an invention which is calculated to make politicians tell the truth; they can no longer make one statement in British Columbia, another in the prairie provinces, another in central Canada and another in the maritimes, because the radio takes the voice from east to west. Therefore hon. gentlemen opposite will have to be very

careful in the objections they are making to this attempt to give Canadian farmers a better deal.
